assets.topic: The Stanford Prison Experiment: Situational Power Over Individual Will
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim conference room in a psychology building. Philip Zimbardo sits before a bank of monitors replaying grainy videotapes from the Stanford Prison Experiment. On one screen, guards in khaki uniforms and mirrored sunglasses bark midnight counts while prisoners in nylon stocking caps shuffle in line; on another, a young guard who smiled in his screening interview now swings a billy club in rhythmic menace. Timecode numbers tick across the corner of each frame.
assets.player_mission: You are the superintendent reviewing the SPE tapes thirty years on. Observe how the mock prison transformed ordinary students into guards and prisoners, then make the call Zimbardo faced: decide when the simulation must stop. Choose answers that reflect the book's claim that situational power dominates individual will.
key_concepts: The Stanford Prison Experiment was a mock prison in which college students were randomly assigned to the roles of prisoner or guard, and the mock prison became all too real.
Situational power can dominate an individual's will to resist, a dominant conclusion of the Stanford Prison Experiment.
The SPE had to be terminated prematurely because the abuses had grown severe.
Zimbardo described his own failure to stop the abuses sooner as 'an evil of inaction.'
Uniforms, anonymity, and the replacement of names with ID numbers stripped prisoners of individuality and empowered the guards.
Reviewing the SPE videotapes was emotionally painful because time had dimmed Zimbardo's memory of the extent of the guards' creative evil and the prisoners' suffering.
Deindividuation, obedience to authority, passivity in the face of threats, self-justification, and rationalization are dynamic processes that can induce good people to do evil.
Zimbardo's curiosity about the darker side of human nature was shaped by his ghetto upbringing in the South Bronx.
Most psychologists have been insensitive to the deeper sources of power in the political, economic, religious, historic, and cultural matrix that defines situations.
The book presents the SPE as an extended case study of the transformation of individual college students as they played their randomly assigned roles.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the power of the situation over individual disposition: the SPE showed that randomly assigned roles plus institutional trappings overwhelmed the participants' will to resist, turning ordinary students into guards and prisoners. Zimbardo grounds this in the videotapes, typescripts, and participant reports he reviews in the Preface, and in his own acknowledged 'evil of inaction.'

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the Preface's central claim: that a host of situational variables — role assignment, uniforms, anonymity, and the institutional script of prison — dominated the participants' will to resist, transforming normal college students into abusive guards and passive prisoners. The boss is the situation itself, whose power the book argues most of us grossly underestimate.
assets.stage_1_observation: The footage shows the second day of the study. Guards wake prisoners with shrill whistles at two in the morning and run the count in a dozen singsong variations. A prisoner refuses to chant with the others and is singled out, while a previously soft-spoken guard tightens his stance and raises his voice. You notice that the guards have stopped using the students' names entirely and call them only by their ID numbers.
assets.stage_1_question: What does this footage most directly demonstrate about the transformation under way?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The pervasive yet subtle power of a host of situational variables — the guard role, uniforms, ID numbers, and the prison setting — is dominating the individuals' will to resist, transforming ordinary college students into guards and prisoners rather than their student selves.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The tape cuts to a prisoner who broke down and sobbed after the guards forced him to sing in front of the others while they laughed. Your graduate assistants warn that the mock prison has become all too real and that the abuse is accelerating. As superintendent, you must decide your next move — the decision Zimbardo faced when the study had to be terminated prematurely.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Terminate the experiment immediately. The situation had overpowered the participants' will to resist, and allowing the abuses to continue would repeat Zimbardo's 'evil of inaction' — the passivity he later identified in his own oversight.

assets.topic: The Bad Barrel vs. Bad Apples: Putting the System on Trial
assets.visual_frame_description: A courtroom-style briefing room where stacks of military investigation reports sit on a long table. Photographs from Abu Ghraib are dimmed on a projection screen. An expert witness in civilian clothes studies a highlighted passage blaming 'absentee landlord' leadership, while across the table a prosecutor in uniform dismisses the document with a wave of his hand.
assets.player_mission: You are the expert witness testifying about the Abu Ghraib abuses. First study what the investigative reports concluded about the causes, then decide how to argue against the 'bad apple' narrative while still holding individual soldiers responsible for their deeds.
key_concepts: The 'bad apple' account treats the Abu Ghraib abuses as the sadistic work of a few rogue soldiers acting on their own.
The investigative reports, chaired by generals and former high-ranking officials, blamed senior officers and 'absentee landlord' leadership for the abuses.
The military and civilian chain of command had built a 'bad barrel' in which a bunch of good soldiers became transformed into 'bad apples.'
Sergeant Ivan 'Chip' Frederick worked the Tier 1A night shift from 4 P.M. to 4 A.M. for forty consecutive nights without a break.
The prosecutor and judge refused to consider that situational forces could influence individual behavior, reflecting the standard individualism conception.
The System is the complex of powerful political, economic, religious, historic, and cultural forces that create the Situation.
Understanding situational and systemic contributions does not excuse a person or absolve him or her from responsibility for immoral, illegal, or evil deeds.
The real power of the System is invariably hidden behind a veil of secrecy.
A full understanding of the dynamics of human behavior requires recognizing the extent and limits of personal power, situational power, and systemic power.
Zimbardo adopts a prosecutorial stance to put the System on trial, because the legal system demands that individuals and not situations or systems be tried for wrongdoing.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the dispositional-versus-situational attribution split at the heart of the book: observers default to dispositional accounts of evil, while the evidence locates causal power in the situation and in the System that builds it. Zimbardo grounds this in the generals' investigative reports and his own expert-witness work on the Frederick case, arguing that the System hides behind a veil of secrecy.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.boss_battle_explanation: This battle tests the book's 'bad barrel' argument: the claim that Abu Ghraib's abuses were not the work of a few rogue soldiers but the product of a barrel built by the chain of command. The deeper boss is the System, hidden behind a veil of secrecy, which Zimbardo puts on trial using the investigative reports and the evidence gathered as an expert witness.
assets.stage_1_observation: You read a section of a report chaired by a retired general. It documents that MP guards on Tier 1A worked the night shift from 4 P.M. to 4 A.M. for forty straight nights without a break, with no senior supervision on site. The report's findings point responsibility upward, at the dysfunctional 'absentee landlord' leadership of the chain of command.
assets.stage_1_question: What do the military and civilian investigative reports identify as the primary cause of the abuses?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The reports laid the blame for the abuses at the feet of senior officers and on their dysfunctional or 'absentee landlord' leadership: the chain of command had built a 'bad barrel' in which good soldiers became transformed into 'bad apples.'
assets.stage_2_intervention: The prosecutor thunders that Sergeant Chip Frederick's abuse was his 'freely chosen rational decision' and demands that you agree the fault was entirely dispositional. You must state your position in front of the court.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Testify that the situational and systemic forces Frederick was embedded in — the forty-night night shift, the absence of leadership, the dehumanizing environment — directly contributed to his abusive behavior, while still affirming that understanding these contributions does not excuse him from responsibility for his actions.

assets.topic: Sergeant Frederick's Self-Justification: Obedience and Rationalization
assets.visual_frame_description: A windowless interview room at a military base. A sergeant in a rumpled uniform sits across from an investigator at a metal table, a tape recorder between them. Photographs of the Abu Ghraib tier are sealed in a folder beside the investigator's elbow. The sergeant's hands stay flat on the table as he speaks in a flat, measured voice.
assets.player_mission: Audit this interrogation. Track Sergeant Frederick's nonverbal behavior and parse his quoted statements, then decide whether his account reflects outright deception or a different psychological process the book identifies. Base your diagnosis on the evidence log and the transcript.
key_concepts: Obedience to authority is one of the dynamic psychological processes that can induce good people to do evil.
Rationalization allows people to reframe harmful acts as duty or necessity rather than wrongdoing.
Sergeant Ivan 'Chip' Frederick was an MP guard at Abu Ghraib and the subject of Zimbardo's expert-witness investigation.
Frederick worked the Tier 1A night shift from 4 P.M. to 4 A.M. for forty nights without a break.
Dehumanization is like a cortical cataract that clouds one's thinking and fosters the perception that other people are less than human.
The standard individualism conception locates the fault entirely in the individual's freely chosen rational decision.
Understanding the situational contributions to behavior does not excuse a person from responsibility for evil deeds.
Zimbardo became an informal psychological counselor for Frederick and his wife, Martha, and was known to them as 'Uncle Phil.'
The prosecutor and judge refused to consider that situational forces could influence individual behavior.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests obedience to authority and rationalization: Frederick's self-justifying account shows how ordinary people absorb the situational frame of a dehumanizing setting and reframe harmful acts as duty. The book's claim is that such self-deception, not premeditated evil, is the typical route by which good people come to do harm.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: During the military investigation, is Sergeant Ivan 'Chip' Frederick knowingly lying about what happened at Abu Ghraib, or is a different psychological process driving his account?
assets.subject_baseline: Frederick is a career military policeman and former corrections officer who served with discipline for years; colleagues and family describe him as steady, rule-bound, and without a prior record of abuse. He worked the Tier 1A night shift from 4 P.M. to 4 A.M. for forty consecutive nights without a break, and he later corresponded emotionally with the author, who became 'Uncle Phil' to the family.
observed_nonverbal_log: 00:00-01:30 — Frederick sits upright with hands flat on the table, speaking in a flat, rehearsed tone; he repeats that he 'did what the job required.'
01:30-03:00 — Asked about the night the 'pyramid' photographs were taken, he looks down at the table, shifts his weight, and blinks rapidly, but keeps his voice level.
03:00-05:00 — He describes the detainees as 'the enemy,' using military jargon; his shoulders relax and his face softens when he frames himself as a soldier rather than a tormentor.
05:00-07:00 — Asked whether he personally chose to pose in the photographs, he pauses, sighs, and answers with the phrase 'orders came down.'
07:00-09:00 — He returns to a calm, detached manner, summarizing that he 'followed the standard operating procedures' on the tier.
interrogation_transcript: Investigator: Were the detainees in those photographs being tortured, Sergeant?
Frederick: I didn't see it that way. They're the enemy. We were doing what the job required.
Investigator: Who told you to take those photographs?
Frederick: (long pause) Orders came down. The guys on the night shift, we all went along. It was the standard way of running the tier.
Investigator: Did you believe at the time that it was right?
Frederick: I believe I did my duty. If the top brass wanted it done differently, they should have said so.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Frederick is not primarily lying; he is self-deceiving through obedience to authority and rationalization. He has internalized the situational frame of the night shift — dehumanized detainees, forty straight night shifts, and no countervailing leadership — so his statements reflect genuine belief rather than fabrication.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The flat, rehearsed affect and the constant military framing suggest he has adopted the identity of an obedient soldier rather than a wrongdoer; the one break in composure — the pause and sigh at the question of personal choice — marks a flicker of dissonance that he immediately resolves by invoking orders. But his refusal to accept personal agency, delivered with calm self-justification, is the hallmark of the book's obedience-to-authority and rationalization processes, not the tell-tale signs of someone concealing known facts.
distractors: Frederick is lying outright to protect fellow night-shift guards and avoid prosecution.
Frederick is suffering stress-related memory loss and genuinely cannot recall the events on the tier.
Frederick is deliberately performing guilt and confusion to win sympathy from the court.

assets.topic: The Veil of Secrecy: Absentee Leadership and Willful Blindness
assets.visual_frame_description: A hearing room where a senior officer in full uniform testifies before investigators at a long oak table. A thick stack of routed memos sits before the questioner, one marked with a red tag. The colonel keeps his back straight and his hands folded as he answers in a measured baritone.
assets.player_mission: Audit this testimony. Study the officer's nonverbal behavior and his exact words, then decide whether his denial that the chain of command knew about the abuses is simple perjury or a subtler process the book describes. Support your diagnosis from the log and transcript.
key_concepts: The real power of the System is invariably hidden behind a veil of secrecy.
The investigative reports, chaired by generals and former high-ranking officials, blamed the abuses on senior officers and 'absentee landlord' leadership.
The chain of command built a 'bad barrel' in which good soldiers were transformed into 'bad apples.'
The standard individualism conception holds that the fault lies entirely in the individual's freely chosen rational decision.
Self-justification and rationalization are among the dynamic processes that can induce good people to do evil.
Understanding situational and systemic contributions does not absolve a person of responsibility for evil deeds.
Zimbardo's prosecutorial stance puts the System on trial because the legal system demands that individuals rather than situations be tried.
A public health approach that changes situations can have a greater impact than remedial action aimed only at individuals.
Senior officers and the civilian command structure share complicity in the abuses at Abu Ghraib.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the systemic-power claim of the Preface: the System hides behind a veil of secrecy and creates the situations in which abuse flourishes, while leaders blame 'bad apples' to preserve their own innocence. The scenario shows willful blindness and self-justification operating at the command level, not as deliberate perjury but as a systemic failure to see.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: A senior officer testifies that the chain of command 'knew nothing' about the Abu Ghraib abuses until the photographs surfaced. Is his testimony deceptive, and if so, what kind of deception?
assets.subject_baseline: Colonel Daniel Marsh (a composite of the senior officers cited in the investigative reports) is a decorated, long-serving officer known for meticulous record-keeping and strict staff discipline. Investigators found that his office was aware of the overcrowding, the night-shift staffing crisis, and early reports of abuse at the prison well before the photographs were released.
observed_nonverbal_log: 00:00-02:00 — Marsh testifies with ramrod posture and an unwavering voice, prefacing each answer with the phrase 'To my knowledge...'.
02:00-04:00 — Asked about specific reports routed to his office, he pauses, blinks, then states that 'paperwork of that sort rarely rises above the battalion level.'
04:00-06:00 — When the investigator reads an excerpt from an earlier abuse complaint, Marsh's jaw tightens and he re-grips the chair arms, but his voice stays measured.
06:00-08:00 — He returns to his refrain that the abuses were 'the acts of a few bad apples,' using the phrase verbatim from the public statement he issued.
interrogation_transcript: Investigator: Colonel, were reports of detainee abuse on Tier 1A ever brought to your attention before the photographs were released?
Marsh: To my knowledge, no. My staff runs a disciplined operation; problems are handled at the lowest appropriate level.
Investigator: This memo dated two months before the photographs is addressed to your office. It describes 'harsh treatment' on the night shift. Do you recognize it?
Marsh: I do not recall this specific document. I have many responsibilities.
Investigator: Should your subordinates have escalated it?
Marsh: My officers are trained to act within their authority. I will not accept that a few bad apples are my personal doing.
assets.correct_diagnosis: Marsh's denial is willful blindness and self-justification enabled by the System's 'veil of secrecy,' not simple, knowing perjury. The investigative reports chaired by generals documented 'absentee landlord' leadership, and Marsh has genuinely convinced himself that because he issued no explicit orders he bears no responsibility — the dispositional 'bad apple' framing that shields the barrel and the System from scrutiny.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The rehearsed 'To my knowledge' hedge, the refusal to engage with a document addressed to his office, and the verbatim reuse of the 'bad apples' talking point all indicate self-protective framing rather than fresh recall; the physiological tension when confronted with the memo shows he recognizes the stakes. His account mirrors the book's argument that the System operates behind a veil of secrecy while leaders retain the standard individualism conception that blame lies in individuals alone.
distractors: Marsh is an honest witness whose subordinates acted entirely on their own initiative.
Marsh is deliberately scapegoating the night-shift MPs to protect one specific senior official.
Marsh has no knowledge of the events because the abuse reports were never routed to his office.

assets.topic: Person, Situation, or System: Sorting the Causes of Evil
assets.visual_frame_description: A sorting board on screen with three labeled columns stacked above a tray of evidence cards. Each card carries a short episode from the book's Preface — a court hearing, a night shift, a ghetto scene, a lab video. The player drags each card into the column where its causal power primarily lies.
assets.player_mission: Sort each factor from the Preface into the level where its causal power primarily operates: the individual's character, the immediate situation, or the overarching System. Then name the level the author argues is the deepest source of the power to create evil out of good.
key_concepts: A large body of evidence in social psychology supports the concept that situational power triumphs over individual power in given contexts.
The System is the complex of powerful political, economic, religious, historic, and cultural forces that create the Situation.
The 'individualism conception' holds that behavior results from freely chosen, dispositional decisions.
Investigative reports described a 'bad barrel' built by the chain of command rather than isolated 'bad apples.'
Dehumanization is like a cortical cataract that clouds one's thinking and fosters the perception that other people are less than human.
Understanding situational and systemic contributions does not excuse a person from responsibility for evil deeds.
The real power of the System is invariably hidden behind a veil of secrecy.
A public health approach that changes situations can have a greater impact than the standard medical model aimed only at individuals.
The rebels who resist the powerful forces of compliance, conformity, and obedience are celebrated as heroes.
assets.theory_summary: This matrix tests the book's three-level explanatory chain — person, situation, and system — and its claim that situational power routinely triumphs over individual power, with the System as the deepest source. The Preface argues that only by recognizing all three levels, and the System's veil of secrecy, can destructive behavior be genuinely changed.

credibility.basis: Classic experimental social psychology (Stanford Prison Experiment, Milgram)

assets.question: For each factor from the Preface, identify where its causal power primarily lies: in the individual's character (the 'bad apple'), in the immediate situation (the 'bad barrel'), or in the overarching System (the 'barrel maker'). Then name the level the author argues is the deepest source of the power to create evil out of good.
assets.column_a_label: Dispositional — the 'bad apple' (individual character and free choice)
assets.column_b_label: Situational — the 'bad barrel' (the immediate setting and its forces)
assets.column_c_label: Systemic — the 'barrel maker' (the political, economic, and cultural matrix)

rows.label: The prosecutor's claim that Sergeant Frederick's abuse was his 'freely chosen rational decision.'
MP guards working the Tier 1A night shift from 4 P.M. to 4 A.M. for forty nights without a break.
Generals' reports blaming senior officers and 'absentee landlord' leadership for the abuses.
South Bronx gang initiations that required stealing, fighting, and intimidating others, normalized as obedience to the group leader.
Landlords and police whose unchecked power could evict families or confiscate a stickball bat without explanation.
Zimbardo's own 'evil of inaction' — his passivity in allowing the SPE abuses to continue.

assets.explanation: The Preface sorts each factor to the level at which its causal power operates, but the book's central claim is that the System is 'the bigger power for creating evil out of good' — the complex of forces that creates the Situation itself. The prosecutor's dispositional reading, the situational forces on the guards, and the systemic structures of ghetto life and command all matter, yet the System operates behind a veil of secrecy and must be confronted for change to be lasting.
distractors: Dispositional causes alone explain why ordinary people do evil.
The situation is entirely independent of the larger System.
The author argues that the System excuses individuals from responsibility for their actions.
